moment I cannot lay my hand on it. Speaking from memory there are at present four paid out of civil government; I think there were four more whom we paid out of the general statistics vote who were practically permanent in the department. Three have been in the department for many years. One is a sort of messenger and typewriter who was appointed several years ago. There are also six employees who have been engaged in working up certain tables from the compilations of the census. That makes altogether fourteen employees in this branch. Of course, none of these are paid out of the census vote, but all are paid out of the general statistics vote, except one or two who are paid out of civil government. There is one officer employed in preparing the criminal statistics. The statistics are secured by arrangement with the judicial officers all over the Dominion, who are paid for sending in the returns. These returns are edited and put into the form of a report, and there is no expense here for compilation except the salary of one clerk. I think he is a junior second-class clerk and is paid $1,100 a year. His salary is charged to civil government. All the others are paid out of the general statistics vote. As being in charge of the general statistics service, I have always had the power-and on different occasions have exercised that power-to instruct the proper officers to draw up such tabulations. It is the duty of the statistical staff to do that work and to do it in a way which will meet, not perhaps, individual demand, but a general demand. My impression is that the commissioners in the various counties will understand much better who are fit and proper persons to appoint as census enumerators, and if the Act is changed in regard to the census of 1901, and made different from what it was in 1891, I think it would be very well to take a backward step. I think the old rule was the best, that is to appoint the commissioner and let the commissioner from amongst the people living in the riding whom he knows well and with whose qualifications he is familiar, name his enumerators without having to fall back on the minister who could not possibly know the men who are qualified to do this work. I am not at all favourable to concentrating all the patronage of the country under the head of a department. I think we had a sufficient illustration of that in the province of Ontario and I am glad to say that the people have condemned it and I think they will condemn it here too. I think it is a bak principle for the government to persistently seek to take power from the people. Seventy-five or a hundred years ago the fight was to obtain power from the Crown and vest it in the people. Here we have a government calling themselves a Liberal government-

and yet they will not allow the people to have anything to say in the administration of their own affairs. That is for the purpose of keeping a string upon the people, of concentrating and centralizing every power that can be possessed under this great ' I ' that we hear so much about. I think it is a mistake and I would advise the hon. minister to go back to the old rule and let the commissioners appoint the enumerators.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext: I am ready to go back to the old rule ; in fact, I have never departed from it. Tlie minister who conducted the census in 1891 followed this very same rule. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) was in the House at that time and he did not object to it. The minister who conducted the census of 1881 under an administration which the hon. gentleman supported for many years carried out that rule and that practice and appointed every enumerator in the Dominion of Canada from the central office at Ottawa. I dare say the rule is wrong. I dare say that the principles which the hon. gentleman is enunciating are right, but if ever there was an occasion when the great ' I ' was repeated and exemplified in this country it was before the present Liberal government came into power.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext: I remember when the census of 1891 was taken. I remember the gentleman who was commissioner in the county which I have the honour to represent, and I am quite satisfied that he appointed his own enumerators. I am not aware that he had to send to Ottawa te have his appointments confirmed ; at any rate he made the appointments himself. There is no doubt about that. Whatever the statute was the practice was different. The practice was that the commissioner appointed his own enumerators, selected hi* own men and appointed them to the work they were to do. If that practice is not consistent with the Bill, then the words applying to the subject should be eliminated, from the Bill so as to leave the appointment of these men in the hands of the commissioners without having to appeal to Ottawa to have these appointments confirmed. It seems to me that it is only dealing fairly with the commissioners and I am quite sure that a better selection will be made if some greater powers are given to the commissioners in the counties, because they certainly know a great deal better who should be appointed than an officer at the) head of the department here. It is quite absurd to say that an officer here should know who is fit in the country to be appointed an enumerator. It is very nice-apparently the hon. minister thinks-to have the honour ofi that patronage. I am not aware that even the representative of the country is permitted in any way to interfere with the commissioner in his appointments. In the county which I have the honour to represent at the present time and which I represented at the time the census of 1891 was taken, I abstained altogether from attempting to influence the commissioner in his selection of enumerators. I think it should be made non-political, that the commissioners should be given a free hand, that these appointments should not be political appointments, but that the best men available should be selected. We are simply providing means to make these appointments purely political appointments, independently of fitness, honesty, or ability to do the work. I would advise the hon. minister to eliminate the words from this clause that vest in him powers to control the appointment of enumerators and tq leave these appointments entirely in the hands of the commissioners.

speechtext:
I would beg to point out to the hon. minister that the statement he has made is not exactly in accordance with the fact. Under the Conservative regime the number of enumerators was very muchi less than under the hon. gentleman's re-i gime. In my own city, for instance, under! the Conservative regime there were four enumerators, while under the hon. gentleman's regime there were fourteen. The difference as between four and fourteen is very great, and when you apply this to the whole of the Dominion of Canada you will see

liow it is that the hon. gentleman has increased the expenditure for the taking of the census. In the first place the census commissioner must collect these enumerators together and instruct them in their duties and for their attendance these men get so much per day. Take fourteen enumerators at $3 per day while obtaining their instructions and it will amount to so much, whereas, in our time, the instructions were, only given to four men. Four men at $3 per day would mean $12 and if the hon. gentleman will multiply 14 by 3 he will see the difference between the two systems. That applies throughout the whole Dominion. The hon. gentleman has not only increased the number of enumerators but he has increased 'their pay, and the result shows the difference between the two systems. The hon. gentleman has stated that section 4 of this Bill is somewhat similar to the "old Act. Section 9 of the old Act is section 4 of the new.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext:

While in the census of 1901, as compared with the census of 1891, you multiplied the number of enumerators, you are, by the Act you are now introducing, going to multiply that to a still greater extent in 1911, and it can only mean the increasing of the cost of taking the census of this country.

On subsection 2 of section 8,-census of Manitoba and parts of the Northwest Territories, to be. taken in the sixth year of each decade.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext: This is to provide for the taking of a five year census in the province of Manitoba which is required by the Subsidy Act of that province, and it also applies the same principle to the provisional territories. If an Act is passed during the present session of parliament constituting these provinces, that would have to be consolidated with this, and the change would be made applying it to the new. provinces. The reason for taking a census in Manitoba every fifth year is that we are required to do so by the Subsidy Act, and I think the same reasoning would apply to the territories or to the new provinces when created. Therefore I have introduced this section, which carries out that requirement.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext:
I quite understand the hon. minister's intention to be that the general census shall be taken all over the Dominion every tenth year. Then subsection 2 makes provision that a census shall be taken in the province of Manitoba and Mr. BLAIN.
the Territories in 1906 and every tenth year thereafter. The intention is quite apparent to my mind, but I am not sure that the language used conveys that intention clearly. speechtext: I would not undertake to give a legal opinion upon that.

speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman should be able to give us a legal opinion, and let us know as a certainty.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext: These clauses were drawn by the Department of Justice, who knew exactly what they were intended to do, and I supposed that they carried out the intention. I may say that I do not consider that subsection 2 can override the main body of the clause, which says that a census of Canada, which means the whole of Canada, including Manitoba and the Northwest Territories, shall be taken in 1911 and every tenth year thereafter. The next clause says that a census shall be taken in a certain portion of the Dominion in 1906 and every tenth year thereafter ; but that does not in any way limit the first part of the clause, or provide that no census shall be taken in the province of Manitoba and the provisional districts in 1911 and every tenth year thereafter. speechtext: I think that in the taking of our census there should be a column for fallow land. I pointed out to the minister some time ago that in none of the censuses of Canada taken hitherto has there been any column of that kind. The minister stated in the House two years ago that the reason for that was that there was now no fallow land of any importance in Canada. The minister could not have given attention to the matter, or he would have known that there is a great deal of fallow land in Canada. There is hardly a farm in Ontario which has not every year from ten to fifteen acres being cleaned and made better for crop in fallow, and I am informed that the same thing is true of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories to some extent, and I suppose of eastern Canada. I think we should have a column for the enumerators to take the quantity of fallow land. It is very important that people intending to come to Canada, should be able to realize, on taking up the census, that Canadian farmers are up to date. But if they find that there is no fallow land in Canada and then take the statement of the Minister of Agriculture, they will come to the conclusion that our farmers do not understand the most advanced methods of cultivation. Every one knows that one of the great essentials for successful farming is to set aside a certain portion for fallow purposes, and it is very important that in the schedule we are now adopting there should be a column showing what land is in fallow.

speechtext: Will the hon. minister explain to what class of public officers he refers in this section ?

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext:
The section refers to any and every public officer in the country,, whether provincial or municipal. That, I believe, is the interpretation that has been put upon the clause, and I do not know that any question has ever arisen under it. The-hon. gentleman will see that it says :

-with or without compensation for so doing, as is regulated from time to time by the Governor in Council.
J understancl it, that contemplates an amicable arrangement with such officials as are referred to. I might cite, as an instance, the collection of criminal statistics. There is an arrangement with the officers of the courts to supply information for pay. A similar arrangement could he made by the office here, as the result of what I might call bargaining with the various provincial and municipal officers for returns of the information they possess.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext: I agree with the minister that this would include officers of the local governments and the municipalities. That being the case, it seems to me we are legislating far beyond our powers as a parliament. The wording of the section, it seems to me, does not bear out the minister's argument. He says an amicable arrangement is contemplated by the wording. Well, if it read ' upon making compensation,' or 1 upon entering into a satisfactory arrangement,' or something of that kind, it would more clearly cover the idea of an amicable arrangement. But the words ' with or without compensation ' may cover a different idea. A municipality may collect, at considerable expense, a large amount of valuable information. It is their own, and they have an absolute right to use it .as they think fit. But if this clause were carried out according to its wording, we would assume the right to expropriate-because that is what it means-the results of their labour and expenditure with or without compensation. I do not think it advisable that this parliament should trench upon the rights of the provinces. It is not wise that, depending upon the chance of an amicable arrangement, we should pass such a clause as this until we have considered carefully, and until the Minister of Justice has considered carefully, the wording of the clause. To me it appears to go clearly beyond our powers and to assume to vest in the Minister of Agriculture authority which this Dominion parliament does not possess. I am in favour of clothing the Minister of Agriculture with all reasonable prerogatives, but I am not in favour of assuming to give him powers beyond the authority of the Dominion parliament.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext: I would not undertake to give a legal opinion on a point of this kind. But I might say that this is a clause that has been on our statute-book since 1879, and, apparently, it has never been called in question or disputed in any way. I think it a power that must be used with discretion And my hon. friend, will notice that it can be exercised only under regulations by the Governor in Council-not by the minister- as is shown by the last part of the clause.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext: So far as the question of expediency is concerned, it is con-

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext: ferring rather wide powers upon the Minister of Agriculture to provide that he may command from provincial officers certain work without compensation. I am inclined to think that parliament has the right to give him that power, but, as a matter of expediency, I would not think it very wise legislation. We have a somewhat similar case in the Franchise Act. According to my recollection, it is provided in that Act that the government here shall have the right to demand from provincial officers copies of lists in their possession, but it can only be done on giving them reasonable compensation, which, if I remember the terms of the statute correctly, was to be regulated by Order in Council. So far as the Dominion officers are concerned, it is quite right that the minister should have power to demand this information of them without further compensation than they already receive. But I would doubt the wisdom of making it apply to provincial officers. It might be advisable that the minister should allow this section to stand for a moment, in order that we may consider that point.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext:
I have no objection to allowing the section to stand for a few minutes. But, as I have said, it has been the law for a long time, and no difficultv has arisen under it. Of course, the power granted must be exercised with great discretion. I think it only fair that when information is required from such officers, due compensation should be given for any trouble they take or labour they perform, and, certainly, for any expense they are put to in furnishing the information. That,,
I think, would always be the plan followed by the Governor in Council. I think this clause is ,more to require the officers to do the work, that we may not be at their mercy as to whether they shall do it or not, or as to the amount of compensation they shall demand. I think it is an authority that is required, and I think the Governor in Council should always be ready to afford reasonable compensation.

BORDEN, On consideration. I would be inclined to the view that the section might pass in its present form. speechtext: My hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Maedonell) desires to make some suggestions with regard toi *section 15, if the minister will allow us to return to it.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext: I desire to draw attention to the fact that the manner of obtaining the information regarding commercial and manufacturing industries is really of an inquisitorial nature. This information has been obtainable at decennial periods in the past ; and I think it is questionable whether it Is a wise provision to give the minister power, every year, to obtain this information regarding commercial and manufacturing interests. We all know that capital is a sensitive creature, and commercial men often decline to give information for various reasons, reasons which I need not point out to the committee. But manufacturers do generally decline to give information about their private affairs, especially when that information is asked for every year. Agricultural information and statistics are of a different nature. But where you have capital invested in large enterprises, joint stock companies and other corporations, I question whether it is a wise provision to have this information collected and tabulated. The concluding part of the section also provides that the minister, in cases where he thinks it advantageous, shall cause such information to be published in such a form as the Governor in Council may prescribe. That provides machinery for the collection and publication of this information. It is, as I have said, of an inquisitorial character, and I would like to ask the minister if similar machinery has been working advantageously in the United States. In any case, I know that in the city of Toronto where this information is partially obtained municipally, great difficulty is experienced in dragging it out from manufacturing enterprises and concerns. If this is an experiment, if it is only pioneer legislation, I doubt its expediency ; if not, will the minister tell us what the experience has been in providing this information for the census in the United States ?

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext:
At present this very system is going on in the United States, although the work is not completed. The permanent census office in the United States
has the same power we are authorized to exercise by this Act, and the same power we have had under the Census Act in census years. I have found myself, and I believe my predecessors have had the same experience, that when information is asked from manufacturing establishments it often happens that they do not understand what use is going to be made of it, and a great deal of hesitation if not indignation is sometimes expressed at what they call the inquisitorial nature of the questions. A number of instances of that kind occurred during the taking of the last census. Wishing to avoid all friction and desiring to proceed cautiously, and with due regard to the feelings of the people, whenever any instance of that kind was reported by one of my enumerators, I sent up a special officer whose business it was to interview the individuals and explain the object of our proceeding. Also we wrote from the central office here a full explanation of the modus operandi of the census, showing to these people that although the information appeared in the schedule as regards their own business, in the published tables it only appeared as information in regard to the whole industry, the whole capital invested, the whole number of employees, the whole amount of products and so on throughout the list ; and nobody could find out on examination of the published compilations what were the facts with regard to any individual industrial establishment. It was also pointed out to them that the original schedules containing all the details of their operations were absolutely secret, and nobody except the officers of the census had any access to them. When that was done their objections were removed, and with the exception of a very few cases, that I could count on the fingers of one hand, all the industrial establishments in Canada freely gave all the information we asked. What my hon. friend says in regard to the collection of this information in Toronto, is quite true, and it is true generally for the! collection of industrial information for the) province of Ontario. But I think that is owing to the fact that they have no authority under the law to extract this information, it is purely voluntary.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext: Not at all, the giving of such authority is entirely a matter for the provincial legislature, it is a matter that concerns property and civil rights within the province, and they have a right to legislate and have legislated upon it, and actually obtain information along those lines.

maintopic: THE ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS BY MINISTERS.
speechtext:
Then I have been erroneously informed. That may be the general law, but I do not think it is a provision under which machinery is operated for getting this information. I am not familiar with the Ontario laws, but I am informed there is no such provision or authority in

108&
the Act under which this information is collected. It may be in the general law of the land, and there may be some provision in the Ontario legislation which, in a general way, gives that power to the government or to the municipality. I quite agree with my hon. friend that at first sight people engaged in industries are averse to giving this information until they are thoroughly satisfied that it is absolutely secret and confidential. When they are so satisfied, their opposition ceases immediately ; and I am sure those people would themselves be the first to take advantage of the information thus acquired when it is published in tables covering the whole country. In regard to the United States, I may say that they have just the same authority we have here, an authority which is given to the Permanent Census Bureau, as it is called there, and they are working under that to-day. I have here a publication regarding the census in the United States, which alludes to that very thing, and shows that it is working satisfactorily.
I think it would be a great pity if an impediment should be put in the way of collecting industrial statistics as well as agricultural statistics. I think that the manufacturing interests of Canada would suffer if there were no such statistics collected. speechtext: I would be very sorry that the hon. gentleman should have such a had opinion of the Bill as to characterize it as a pirate Bill, and to say that it is pioneer legislation and so on and so on. I do not thiifk there is anything in the nature of a black flag or skull and cross bones in the legislation. Certainly this clause is not pioneer legislation. This power and authority have been given to the Department of Agriculture under the Census Act ever since we have had a census taken in Canada. It has been given in every country in the world where a census is taken. It is one of the absolute essentials of the collection of statistics. If you want to secure information and if you have no power to require the information your statistics are simply worthless because your information is not complete. Any bad natured or sulky individual in the community, or any small group of individuals could at any time defeat the whole object of the investigation if it were allowed at the caprice of an individual or a group who entertained some peculiar ideas as to their particular rights to refuse to give the information. That is one of the essentials of census taking. My hon. friend says that this is pioneer legislation. We have had the same kind of thing exactly in our Census Act for thirty or forty years.

It has been working in regard to other things since 1902, and in the United States before that this same principle was applied to the taking of the census every ten years. I have here the report of Mr. Cortelyou who was the secretary of the Department of Commerce and Labour in the United States until quite recently and who had the management of this census. In this report he refers to the taking of the industrial census which is going on in the United States, and he takes credit to his bureau and to himself for doing this work and for requiring this information. hon. friend is quite right in saying that this is pioneer legislation and that it has not been tried. In the United States the inquiries made and the information collected have become exceedingly detailed because in the United States they have a law against trusts and combinations which we have not here. The inquiry at present being held into Industrial affairs is. I think, being held by the Bureau of Corporations which is a Mr. FISHER.
branch of the permanent Census Bureau, a new institution, in order to be able to apply with some degree of efficiency the law against trusts and combinations. It is necessary for the Bureau of Corporations to have this inquisitorial power which they have in the United States, under almost the same wording as we find here in section 15. But here we have no law against trusts and combinations, and it seems to me that until we have such a law-and I believe we are approaching a time when we must have that law-it is fair for us to ask that we should know exactly what kind of information will be asked from us. A very interesting report has been made by Mr. Garfield, the chief of the Bureau of Corporations, who is proceeding with this inquiry regarding industrial progress and industrial conditions in the United States. He has called into operation that power which my hon. friend (Mr. Fisher) is seeking to take here by section 15, and he had to ask from certain classes of manufacturers, or certain manufacturers in certain parts of the United States, questions which have not hitherto been asked, and which were not found in the usual schedules, such as the cost of production of the articles manufactured, the wages paid, the prices at which they sell an article in different parts of the United States, and the prices at which they sell in foreign countries. Mr. Garfield says that the securing of that information is absolutely necessary for him in order to place the government in such a position that it will be enabled to enforce the anti-trust and anti-combination laws. Section 15 has a foot note leading us to suppose that it is taken from Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 59, sections 1 and 2. Therefore, we are to assume that there is no material change-in other words, that this is not what the minister speaks of as pioneer legislation. Let me say that upon looking at this section, I find that we are having pioneer legislation of a very dangerous character, if the provision of the original section was necessary. That the minister may appreciate the importance of this, let me call his attention, in the first place, to the fact, that section 15 provides for the collection not only of agricultural, commercial, educational and manufacturing statistics, but also of criminal statistics. Then, part 4 of the Bill provides specially for the collection of criminal statistics, but in this case a special safeguard is provided, for section 2t>

The Minister of Agriculture shall, from time to time, subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, make such regulations and prescribe such forms as appear necessary and expedient, for the purpose of collecting, abstracting, tabulating and publishing vital, agricultural, commercial, criminal and other statistics, and such rules, regulations and forms, when assented to by the Governor in Council and published in the ' Canada Gazette,' shall have the force of law.
