House in Committee of Supply.
Public buildings, Quebec-Acton Vale public building, $8,000.

This, Mr. Chairman, is to complete the payments on the public building at Acton Vale in the county of Bagot. The contract for the building was let on the 28th of June of last year for $10,250. The population of the town and parish to be served by the office is 3,000.

I would like to say in a general way in connection with these public buildings and without my remarks being especially applicable to the public building at Acton Vale and without going over the ground that was gone over yesterday in connection with our system of procedure in regard to public buildings, that I have looked over the list of public buildings in the province of Quebec, and I find that there are 12. 13 or 14 public buildings as regards which I doubt if there has ever been any urgent demand upon the government for their construction, otherwise than by the desire exhibited by the sitting member to have a public building. I think that is about the genesis of the public building.-1 have seen many of these buildings in Quebec and I suppose they are the same ail over Canada-and it bears the date of itsl erection and the name of the minister prominJ cntly displayed; sometimes it bears the narnq of tlie sitting member, and the expectation oti the sitting member is that if he gets a public; building he will consolidate himself in the constituency. As a matter of fact a number of members have declared to me that public buildings have been the cause of untold bitterness to them.
It works the other way.

Generally it works the other v ay. The locality chosen gives rise to a good deal of bickering and heart-burning
and often there are several possible sites chosen and the ultimate choice of the location leads to a lot of heart-burning. The contractor who erects the building finds many enemies for the sitting member and the man who is placed in charge of it generally makes a great many enemies for the sitting member also. That is what I have noticed in regard to public buildings since I have been in this House. The hon. member for .South Toronto (Mr. Maedonell), I think, pointed out what has been a ground of complaint since 1896. that there is no system in regard to public buildings, there is no rule and as a general thing we never have any information here in regard to these public buildings. I have heard time and time again the predecessors of my hon. friend tell us that such and such a sum which we were voting would finish certain public buildings, and the next year we were called upon for a new appropriation for the same buildings.
I have asked for plans time and time again, before we started on a public building, and I have never been able to obtain them nor much other information which is absolutely necessary in order to proceed in a businesslike way to the execution of this policy of building public buildings, if it may be called a policy. Take the public buildings in Quebec for this year and we have no data ; my hon. friend will admit that. My hon. friend (Mr. Hyman) is a stranger to the province of Quebec.
A foreigner.

Not a foreigner but a stranger, and I would not like to ask him a number of questions in regard to these public buildings which would prolong debate uselessly. As a matter of fact, many of the constituencies where many of these public buildings are to be erected are not even represented here to-night and probably the bitterness of which I spoke a moment) ago is already in the souls of the members who have asked for these public buildings. We will vote to-night for the class of public buildings I have alluded to, some $500,000, about $200,000 for public buildings in localities that I am perfectly sure could be benefited infinitely more by another kind of expenditure. We will vote a couple of hundred thousand dollars to complete what t To complete a sum I have no hesitation in saying of about $600,000, nearly three quarters of a million dollars, in order to finish these public buildings, and when we have spent $750,000 or $600,000 or perhaps more than three quarters of a million dollars on these public buildings erected in localities of which I will say a word in a moment, we will have made a permanent charge upon the public revenue of nearly $60,000 a year. If my hon. friend (Mr. Hyman) will take these'public buildings and have an estimate made of what they cost for repairs, gas, heating, and caretakers. I think I am making a moderate estimate in saying that he will find that it will cost us about $60,000

a year to maintain these public buildings. I am equally certain that I am within the limit of reason in saying that for the purpose for which these public buildings are being erected $60,000 a year of rental would give the public all the accommodation they) required. I am prepared to go carefully over each of these localities-I am not speaking of the city of Quebec or Montreal or Three Rivers, but of the smaller places- and to say that with $60,000 a year we would secure sufficient accommodation for all the public services and be free in each case to change the office to lease more space and sol forth. In these small localities the important part of the town is often changing. I could point out a number of public buildings in Quebec that were probably erected in the right places when they were erected, but which are not now in the most suitable part of the town. But they are there to stay and to remain a charge upon the public treasury. Yet if the government to-day wished to secure accommodation in the same towns it would probably erect buildings elsewhere. I desire very much to emphasize this fact, that I am not opposed tot public buildings in any of these particular smaller localities ; not at all. If the Minister of Public Works wished to put up ai public building in every locality in my own county I would not refuse.
As a matter of fact, when I was younger in public life, I think it was in 1901, I called the attention of the then Minister of Public Works to the fact that he was putting up no public building in my own constituency, where one might be of use, and he promised to take the matter into his serious consideration. The ground I take is that we could spend the same amount of money in these constituencies with much better result than by continuing what I am told has been the slipshod policy of every government, of putting up a public building merely to satisfy a particular member, because a previous government had put up one in another constituency. Now, I have looked over this list of appropriations for public buildings in my own province, and I believe that in many of these instances, if the people at large were consulted as to whether they would prefer to have a public building in one of the villages-because most of them are villages-or to have some other improvement which would benefit the whole constituency, there would not be a moment's hesitation. Our policy regarding public buildings is one that rests very often upon the vanity or the individual ambition of the sitting member to do as much as some other man has done. For instance, take the first place mentioned, that is, Acton Yale, in the county of Bagot, a very strong agricultural constituency, where much dairying is successfully carried on.
I have no hesitation in saying that we could do much more for that constituency in the field of agriculture than by putting Mr. MONK. .
up a public building at Acton Vale. What is the great complaint in Montreal and the other centres from which butter is shipped ? It is that our present system of bonus-ing the steamship and railway companies to provide cold storage facilities for the conveyance of perishable goods is faulty- why ? Because these companies would be obliged under any circumstances to provide accommodation for perishable products, particularly butter. Our produce men in Montreal say that the government, instead of spending so much in bonusing these companies, which must supply cool space for the purposes of their business, should give some aid to the farmers who after bringing their butter to the stations, are obliged to leave it there sometimes three or four hours in the sun and subject to great deterioration. It has been urged upon me very often in Montreal that the government had much better devote some money to the erection of cooling rooms or small ice houses at the principal depots where butter is received. That would benefit, not a particular locality or a particular contractor or a certain set of men, but the entire district. Then, improvements might be made in the mail service. If the hon. minister were to offer, as I do not think he will, either to put up a public building in my own constituency or to spend the same amount of money on improving the mail service, I have no doubt that my constituents would not hesitate for a moment to say, give us an improper mail service, or do what this government has been urged again and again to do-reduce the indebtedness to the government of the Montreal Turnpike Trust; and you will benefit all the farmers throughout the constituency. Then, everybody knows that, for the development which we require in most of these counties where public buildings are going to be erected, important railway communications are required ; and I have no doubt that if the same amount of money were expended on improving the railway communications, a far greater benefit would be bestowed upon the people. I do not apply these remarks to large centres like Montreal and Ottawa. Consider the immense amount of money we are spending yearly in rents in Ottawa, I think over $30,000, with departments spread all over the city. It seems to me that it would be better for us to install properly the central offices of administration than to squander money all over the country in that way. I have given utterance as briefly as possible to the view which I have entertained for many years of the policy of the government in regard to public buildings. I quite agree with what has been said, that if we adhere to that policy, it would be a great convenience for us to have a clearer statement of the stage at which the work has arrived on each of these public buildings, of the site and of the plan, as we .ought to have a eer-

tainty that the expenditure will not go beyond a certain fixed sum in any particular place. But there is no such rule. I make these observations because I know that candidates in the fever of an election contest take up any utterance that we have made here in connection with the erection of public buildings, and invoke it before the people in order to prejudice them against us. Therefore I do not see the use of singling out any particular building. The remarks I have made apply to all, and I thought it well to make them in the first instance in order to facilitate the business of the committee.

In answer to the hon. gentleman, 1 have to say, in the first place, that with regard to every building for which the government is taking a vote, there has been a very clear and concise statement made of the estimate by the chief architect, and all the details ; and I will endeavour to see that the expenditure does not go beyond the amount voted, although there are often contingencies arising in building operations to make it impossible to keep the cost entirely within the estimate. For the first time, I think, we have learned the secret of some of the opposition given in the House to this expenditure. The hon. member for Jacques Gartier takes exception to the custom that prevails in the province of Quebec of putting certain names on the buildings. He says it is customary to put on a building the name of the member representing the constituency in this House, and also the name of the minister. Possibly I may soften his opposition to this particular building by assuring him that I shall be glad to forego the honour of having my name placed upon it, and that I should be very glad indeed to place upon it the name of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier if he thinks that will in any way add to the lustre and honour of his name after he departs from this sphere. With regard to the system of erecting public buildings, that did not originate with this government; it has been in existence for many years. As I said last evening, if you consider the system purely and simply from the dollars and cents standpoint, I have no doubt that it cannot be defended entirely as a business proposition. But it has been the custom, I think ever since confederation, to lay aside a certain amount of money for the construction of these buildings. With regard to the particular building at present under the consideration of the committee, I do not know what other expenditure could possibly be made in the county of Bagot. It is an inland county, in which there has never been any expenditure on wharfs or other public works. The hon. gentleman says that the money might be spent in improving the mail service. I feel quite sure that if the people of Bagot have any complaints to make in regard to the mail service, my
hon. colleague the Postmaster General will see that these complaints are remedied. The hon. gentleman referred to the question of a public building in his own county. Well, I shall be very glad to give every consideration to anything the hon. gentleman may lay before the department on that subject; but after his gloomy picture about the granting of public buildings, and the bickerings and heart burnings which he says occur in most constituencies where public buildings are erected, I am sure he would not care to have one erected in his constituency.
As to public buildings in Montreal, Toronto and the other large cities of the Dominion, there can be no question of doubt in regard to the policy of the government. But I must say that I am not prepared, nor, I think, is the government prepared, to subscribe to the idea that, having provided buildings for these cities, we must stop at that. I believe that care ought to be exercised ; but there are so many considerations that govern the decision as to erecting public buildings in smaller places that it is almost impossible to lay down a rule. The matter was discussed many a time when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, and they never were able to lay down a rulei that could be always adhered to, nor do I think that any such rule could be framed.
Would the minister please state the post office and the customs revenue.
The postal revenue for the year last reported was $949. There is no customs house there at present.
Is it intended to establish a customs house there ?

I understand that it is.
Chicoutimi public building, $15,000.

The site chosen for this building is a very desirable one and cost about $2,400. It is intended to put up a building there that will cost, for the building proper $21,000, and for the whole structure, including heating, wiring, fittings, &c., $30,000.
Is the present appropriation intended to complete the work?
No, I have just explained that, we are to spend $30,000 and so we must ask for another vote.

I ask, because last year, $8,000 was voted for this building and $4,000 spent. This vote will make a total of $19,000. The minister started last year with $8,000, then asked for enough to increase that to $19,000, and now we have a prospect of $30,000 expenditure.

Not a prospect-a certainty,	*	,

110S

I ask this, as I wish to do on every occasion, because I think it is the duty of the minister to tell us, not what he wants for the season, but what he expects ultimately to spend on the work. I think if that rule were followed on every occasion, we should have a little more sense of responsibility on the part of ministers.

The first vote was for $8,000. We are now asking for $15,000. I have already put it on 1 Hansard ' that it is the intention of the government to spend for this building $30,000. Of necessity, therefore, the government must ask for another vote to make up the total, and that vote will be asked for in the main estimates or, in the supplementary estimates, of next year.

What is the population of Chicoutimi, and why is a $30,000 building required there ? I do not profess to know much about the business of Chicoutimi. I was there a great many years ago. X am not aware that it has made any wonderful progress. This vote of $30,000 compared with the appropriations in other parts of the Dominion seems a very large sum and should call for some explanation.

I had the pleasure of visiting Chicoutimi, one of the few places I have been able to visit since I undertook the work of the department. Chicoutimi is advancing very rapidly indeed. It has now, I am informed, a population of about 6,000 or 6,400. A number of important interests have been centering there, and X have no doubt that when it is made, the great practical terminus of the Lake St. John Railway, it will become a very much larger town than it is at present. The lot on which the building is to be placed makes it necessary to construct a building rather more than usually expensive. The lot has streets on every side, and it is in a very prominent place. Every passenger getting off the boat, and every person who comes to Chicoutimi must see the public building. There are practically four fronts, each of which must have a certain amount of ornamentation. This will make it necessary to spend $2,000 or $3,000 more than would otherwise be spent.
What is the postal and customs revenue ?

The postal revenue is $3,-< 085, and the customs about $8,000. I may say that it is intended that this building shall also afford accommodation for the government telegraph service and engineering department.
Public buildings, Quebec-Dominion buildings -renewals, improvements, repairs, &e., $12,000.

How is it intended to apply this amount ? We vote every year for the public buildings of Quebec $12,000, and every year we spend that amount. A strange coin-j cidence. What is it intended to do with the money this year ?

The vote is always $12,0001 but I do not know that the expenditure will be $12,000 exactly. I have no data to show exactly where this money is to be spent. It depends upon contingencies that may arise and the decision of the architect with regard to them.
Grosse Isle quarantine station-improvements and repairs to buildings, &c., $12,000.
This is called for by the Department of Agriculture, which depart-) ment, as the committee is aware has charge of Grosse Isle.

An amount was voted last year, and we were told specifically what it was for. According to my recollection the installation of a fresh water system was one item of expenditure. What is to be done with the present vote ?

It is partly a continuance of the work last year. Money has been or is to be spent on police quarters, drainage, plumbing, hospital fire escape, painting superintendent's residence, new quarters for sailors, plank walks and other items-it is a general vote.
But this year we do not require to do that work.
Only a part of the work has been done. In this item there is completion of the quarters for sailors, an ice house, well, repairs to medical superintendent's residence and other items.

Will this vote finish every-; thing except the ordinary repairs that go on from year to year ? ' Improvements and repairs ' is a very general expression. The hou. minister can easily spend $100,000 on * improvements.'

I am not in a position to promise the House that there will be no more improvements at Grosse Isle. 1 do not know whether the hon. member (Mr. Barker) has visited Grosse Isle, but I was there some time ago, and I must say that some of the buildings are not in a good state of repair, and must, in time, be renewed. Soi far as the Department of Public Works is concerned, it has no intention of asking more than this vote. But the hon. gentleman will understand that if the department in control of the quarantine station come to the Public Works Department and say that the accommodation is not sufficient and show good reason why a new building should be constructed, I am sure the hon. gentleman himself, considering the importance of that quarantine station, would not ask the department to pledge itself not to ask for another vote.
The hon. minister misunderstood me. I am aware that repairs will be needed every year.

And renewals-there may be renewals.
<

Government buildings are, or ought to be, of a very substantial character, and so they should not require to be renewed frequently. But X admit that repairs are constantly needed, because government buildings should be kept in the best condition of repair. I do not dispute that for a moment. But when we have the word ' improvements ' stuck on every year, $12,900 last year, $12,000 this year, and so on, I think we ought to know when this is going to end.

The hon. gentleman's remarks might apply to public buildings of the. character we have been discussing a little while ago, but they do not apply to this case. These buildings are wooden buildings, or a large number of them; some of them have been in existence for forty-seven years. Under these circumstances, no doubt, they will have to be frequently repaired and renewed. It is the intention of the department to repair and renew them. Except for these purposes the department does not expect to have to apply for further appropriations in the way of buildings.
You are prophesying.
Of, course, if the Agriculture Department makes a demand for works we have to supply them.
My hon. friend will regret very much that he made such a promise. I think for the last twenty-five years these improvements have been on the estimates.
How much was expended last year on headquarters for sailors ? I understood that in the vote last year a certain amount was to be expended on headquarters for sailors. How was the money expended?

It was expended by day labour. If the hon. gentleman knew the circumstances, he would know that we have to house all the men employed there and provide accommodation for their families, $8,001) was spent last year, and we require some $6,000 more to complete that building.
Last year we were told that $8,000 would complete; how is it the hon. gentleman comes forward now and asks for $6,000 more?	-

I understand that last year it was hoped that we would be able to put up this building on the same kind of foundation as was under the other building. But when the matter was further investigated it was found that this building, which was 150 feet long by 32 feet wide, would require to stand on a heavier foundation than the other buildings. That is the explanation of the increased cost.
How mucii money was spent last year on plumbing?
I read out in detail the whole of the expenditures for last year.
This will complete the work ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes, according to the estimates submittal hy the Department of Agriculture.
Last year the minister asked for $12,000 to be voted and stated to the committee that it would complete the work. That is only a few months ago. Now, the hon. gentleman comes forward and, in a case where $8,000 was asked for last year to complete the work, he asks for $6,000 more. It is not to be wondered at that the representatives from Quebec are anxious to know when this work will be finally completed. My hon. friend will remember that for this plumbing he has mentioned this evening, about the same amounts were voted last year, with which he promised to complete the plumbing. One would imagine there were extensive buildings going up there every year. Preparation of the plans and specifications on which the estimates are based, would seem to show some recklessness in the department somewhere.

I see the point the hon. gentleman is trying to make. Last year the Minister of Public Works made certain statements to the effect that the vote he asked for would complete the plumbing, and it did not complete it. He had an estimate given by the architect of the department, which it was supposed would complete. But it does not follow that the amount voted last year would complete for this year. As I stated, there were old buildings which naturally require renewal and repairs. This is a very necessary work, at any moment we are liable to have 1,000 or 2,000 people landed on that island.

It is quite true that I am not acquainted with that island, but when the minister comes forward and makes a statement that $8,000 is to be expended for headquarters for sailors, and promises that it will complete the work, and then comes forward the next year and asks for $6,000 more, and without explaining the reason-
I am sure the hon. gentleman does not wish to he unfair. He asked me for explanations and I gave them.

I do not wish to misrepresent the hon. gentleman, but I ask him to be more careful in the preparation of his estimates. The committee does not wish to hold him down to exactly $8,000, we would not complain if he exceeded it by a few hundred or a thousand, but when he asks for $6,000 more, almost as much again, it does look either as if his officers were reckless

in the preparation of the estimates or as if the minister was not very careful in making statements before the committee. The committee is quite willing to vote the necessary money, so far as we are concerned, but we are anxious that the hon. gentleman should be more careful in preparing his estimates.
Were these amounts spent by day work ?
Yes.
I see here a certain amount for electric lighting, Ahearn & Soper, Ottawa. Isn't that going far from Quebec for such things?
Some of these articles come from the United States.
They can be got in Quebec. I see also an item for wheelbarrows from Frost & Wood in the province of Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They have an agency in Quebec.
What county is that in!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Montmagny.
I see that they have been repairing some steamers there.
Yes ; we repair the ' Challenger ' there every year.
That is one of the expenses in connection with that place ?

Yes.
Lachute public building, $10,000.
Will my hon. friend give us some explanation about this ?

This is a vote for the purpose of erecting a public building in La-chute, in the county of Argenteuil. The site has not been procured for the building yet, but it is intended to procure a site at an early date. There are some negotiations going on in regard to several sites. We are trying to get options on two or three sites.
How much are the site and building expected to cost ?

I cannot give the information in regard to the site. In a town of any size a difference of thirty or forty feet will make a difference of at least a thousand dollars in the cost of a site. We always try to meet the wishes of the inhabitants of towns and cities, and I do not know what we may have to do in this case. We will buy the best site available for the building.
Will this amount complete the work ?
No.

How much will it cost for the purchase of the site and the erection Jfr. BLAIN.
and equipment of the building ready for occupation ?

I have endeavoured to explain to the hon, gentleman that I cannot venture any prediction or estimate as to the cost of the site. I want to be perfectly frank with the committee, and I want to be left to exercise some judgment in regard to where the site ought to be. Therefore, it is impossible for me to give any estimate in reference to the site.
Have you no estimate in regard to the building ?

I expect to be able to put up a building there for about $13,000. I might explain that we have made careful estimates of several classes of buildings, which we designate in the department as A, B, G and D ; and when a public building is to be erected, I simply say that we will put up building A, B, C or D, as the case may be. It depends, of course, on the locality in which the building is to be erected as to the cost. The same building in one locality will cost $2,000 or $3,000 more than in another locality. I propose to put up what we call building B in Lachute.
When is it intended to commence the work ?

Just as soon as we can get a site. It is intended to advertise for tenders immediately.
Levis public building, $30,000
Is this building under contract ?
The building is under contract.
Who has the contract ?
Mr. J. Couture, of Levis.

Have you bought the site t
. Mr. HYMAN. By some arrangement with the Railway Department we have acquired a site for this building.
What will be the size of the building ?
64 by 45 feet; two and a half stories, with an annex 34 by 30 feet J pressed brick on a stone foundation.
I suppose this will be the ordinary building to accommodate the post office, customs and inland revenue ?
It is to cover all the departmental wants of the town.
What will the total cost of this building be when it is finished ?

The contract for the building is $22,000 ; heating, $2,500 ; and electric wiring and fixtures, $1,500. The furniture and fittings will depend upon the num-i ber of letter boxes that may be decided on

after the building is completed. We have to ask the Post Office Department as to the number of boxes they will require, and for that we have figured $4,000 or $4,500. For sidewalks, if it is found that there is any necessity for replacing sidewalks, we estimate $500, and, with contingencies, it is figured that the building will cost $33,000 or $34,000.	[DOT]
Was the building let by tender ?
Yes, the work was let by tender, and the contract was given to the lowest tenderer.
When is it to be completed?
On the 30th October, 1906.
How much did the site cost?
I have just explained that the site cost nothing. It came from the Railway Department.
Government land ?

Intercolonial Railway land.
Longueuil public building, $11,000.

What class of building is this-A, B or C ? This distinction, which the hon. minister made a few moments ago, is the first one I have ever heard in connection with this policy of erecting public buildings.
This building has been under contract for some time, and this amount is to complete it.

This new classification of buildings has not been discussed or mentioned in this House before. I would like to ask the hon. minister whether he has plans, details and specifications of each of these four classes of buildings, because if he has made a classification of this kind, it would simplify our work a great deal if he would place on the table plans, details and specifications of each of these four classes of buildings. Then all we would want to know would be as to whether such and such a class of building had been adopted.

Notwithstanding the fact that the Department of Public Works may put up a building which we term A in a certain locality for a certain sum, we may not be able to put up the same building at another point for the same sum, but we adhere to the cost of the building as nearly as possible. In erecting the same building in two different localities we have found a difference of $3,000 in the cost of a $20,000 building. It depends on wages, the question of the availability of stone, the cost of brick and other local considerations. Within a distance of a hundred miles there may be a difference of between 10 and 15 per cent in the cost of the building. I understand the desire of the committee to be to
as nearly as possible, arrive at what the department expects to spend on a particular work. I have endeavoured to reach a standard, and it is as close a standard as I have been able to get.
What is the cost of each of these classes of buildings-A, B, G and D ?
Building A would be a small building which we would put up where there is nothing but a very small post office.
B ?

B would be a building where the accommodation would be somewhat greater, and C where there would be a customs house in addition to post office. In addition to that, we have to consider the question whether we have a Public Works office in the town or not.
Magog public building, $10,000.
Is that completed ?
No, it is not begun yet.
Will the minister give us an explanation of this?
This is a vote of $10,000 towards the completion of a public building at Magog.
I understood it was not commenced?
Neither is it. The $10,000 is a vote for the completion of the building.
What does the site cost?
We have not bought a site yet but we are negotiating at the present time.
What class of building is this?

The postal revenue at Magog is $2,527, and the customs revenue is $3,009. The population is 3,516. The building we expect will cost $21,500 to complete. It is a building with a stone foundation with a brick superstructure.
Who has devised that kind of building? I have remarked it in many places. It is stone for the first story and brick above.
Not always.
I may say that it makes a very bad appearance. I do not know who has invented that building or why it was decided to make these buildings in that way.

I am sorry we have offended the artistic eye of my hon. friend, but I have always understood that the public buildings put up not only by this government but by the late government under the

present chief architect and his predecessors compared, as a whole, very favourably with the buildings of the larger corporations. I do not think the committee would desire to put up a building costing .$20,000 with a brick foundation. I think the extra cost is warranted by the longer life of the building and the lower expense for repairs.

We will come later to some buildings which I -want to discuss. I think that this class of building is an eyesore in some cases and I do not think it would cost more to make the buildings all nice brick or stone. I must say that the buildings which have been put up by this government are not at all to be compared with those erected by the late government. I do not know if they cost as much. Take for example the public building at Sorel, which is really a very nice building.
It is an all stone building.
That is what I am saying; I do not think it costs much more and it looks a great deal nicer than the new ones.

This I understand is in Stanstead county. The first knowledge we had of this was an item of $5,000 asked by the Minister of Public Works to put up a public building at Magog. The minister said that the building would cost $12,000 but now the acting minister comes forward and says it will cost $21,000.
No.

What does my hon. friend
say?

The hon. gentleman says it will cost that amount. I said that the estimate of the department of the cost of the building is that amount but in addition to that there are the boxes, the fittings and the heating.

The peculiar feature of this is that generally there is a vote for a public building a year before an election in a constituency, and then nothing is done. Parliament votes $10,000, as in this instance, for the immediate construction of a building, but nothing is done, the election takes place there is a terrible scuffle about the site and the whole thing is put off from year to year.

Of necessity the votes we are asking now were asked last year. Every vote, practically, in the estimates is a vote that was initiated last year except for buildings that have been running more than one year.
I misunderstood the hon. gentleman then. I understood him to say that the total cost of the building and site would be about $21,000.

I have said that $21,000 is the estimate of the cost of the building. I Mr. HYMAN.
have said that when the site is not purchased it is impossible to put any estimate on it as a few feet difference in the position of the site makes a difference in its cost. I estimated that the building would cost about $14,000 that is, for the contract itself; the heating would cost $2,500 and if there is any wiring to be done it will cost $500. and the fittings are estimated to cost $2,500. We will have to get from the Post Office Department the number of boxes that will be necessary. Renewals of sidewalks, &c., may cost $500 and contingencies $1,500, making a total of $21,500.
My hon. friend says $21,500. The first statement by the minister (Mr. ,T. Sutherland) was $12,000 and at another place he says $25,000.
I am cutting it down.
My hon. friend is getting economical but he has not bought the lot, I notice. I wish the minister would be a little more careful in the statements he makes to the committee.
What statement does my hon. friend object to?

I am not objecting to the statements the hon. gentleman himself makes, but I suppose he is responsible for the statements made by the minister (Mr. J. Sutherland). In the selection of a site I suppose that, as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier suggests, the members are perhaps consulted.
Why not?
Because the hon. gentleman does not consult the members on this side, and he is supposed to be non-political in the expenditure of public money.
I should be glad indeed to consult the members.
Perhaps he might explain whether it is the ' A,' 'B' or ' C ' building that will be erected in constituencies represented by hon. members on this side of the House.
I would like to have a 1 B ' building.

I understood the minister (Mr. J. Sutherland) to say that it was supposed $500 or $1,000 would be paid for the site. What I find fault with is that we do not have the same statements in successive years. We have a variety of Minister of Public Works and each minister has a different statement.
And we are getting worse all the time.

One minister makes a statement on which his estimate is passed and the gentleman who succeeds him enlarges a little on that. That has been the general history of the Department of Public

Works. In the general elections the candidates assist the ministers in promising their constituents public buildings. They generally have a promise of a post office or public building on which they ask support; occasionally they have a private letter in their pockets which they show to their friends privately, but they have not the courage to produce the letter publicly so that their opponents could get a chance to see whether the Minister of Public Works takes a hand in promising these buildings. I think it is high time that this sort of thing should stop; let us fight these matters on fair grounds. If a public building is really necessary in any place I am sure the opposition will assist in passing estimates for all reasonable expenditure, but it is like striking below the belt when government supporters have, these private letters in their pockets and endeavour to make votes in that way.
Public building Montmagny, $10,000.
Will the minister state what he proposes to do about this building*
I propose to put up a new one.
Then you will throw the old building down. Remember that it has fallen down itself. How much money do you propose to spend on it ?
I hope to be able to put up a building there at a cost of about $10,000.

I do not wish to be hard on the minister or to prevent that building being erected ; but I wish to tell him that there has been a regular farce about that building for the last six years. In the first place, there was a building there, and our friend Choquette took a friend there, and he got the government to buy that building for $7,000. To hear him talking in the House, you would suppose that it was a first-class building ; but the postmaster was id it for only about a year and a half when the whole thing went down on his back. The foundations were no good, and the building went down three or four years ago, and every year since there has been $5,000 or $6,000 asked for a new building. How soon will you put it up ?
We are going to put up a new one.
Will you have a good foundation ?
I promise the hon. gentleman that we will try to have a good foundation. I understand that the other was a little shy of foundation.
Ask the postmaster how shy he was when he got caught. It was very lucky for Mr. Choquette that he was not there.
I will see that the foundation shall have the particular care of the department.

The ground there is very soft, and you should go deep enough and put up a good building ; and after you have' it built, do not ask us for any more money. Ask enough now.
Montreal barracks for permanent corps, $20,000.
Where is that going to be built ?

This vote is put in to enable the department to start the work. There has been no decision as to the location of the barracks, nor am I able to state at the present moment the exact size of the building.
Has the minister any idea of how much it will cost ?
I am not able to state the exact amount. It depends on the number of men, the quarters and the character of the building. If I am pressed closely in regard to this vote, I must ask to let it stand.

I thought the minister had some idea of the cost, because this has been spoken of in Montreal for about eighteen months. I may say that I do not see any politics in this at all. The building is very much wanted. I understand that there has been some correspondence between the city council or the authorities of Montreal and the Department of Militia and Defence. Perhaps the Minister of Marine and Fisheries can enlighten the House on this subject. I imagine that as soon as the site is chosen the work will be commenced ; for I do not suppose the government have put the amount in the estimates simply to make people believe that they intend to do so.

May I suggest that possibly it will meet the views of the hon. gentleman to allow the vote to pass, with the understanding that at any time when the estimates of the Minister of Militia are up the information may be asked from him.

I think the Minister of Marine and Fisheries may be able to give us some information on this matter, which is one of considerable interest in Montreal. I understand that under the agreement the city of Montreal is to furnish the site. For my part, I have no objection to the item passing, but I think we should have some explanation as to how far the negotiations have proceeded. One site suggested was behind the mountain and another east of the city.

I am aware that ten years ago the city of Montreal voted $25,000 towards the erection of this military

school building. The matter has been in abeyance since. The military authorities have represented that it is necessary to go on with the enterprise, and last year, before the elections, it was about concluded that the school would be placed at Point aux Trembles where the shooting grounds are. Later it was'represented that the site was not near enough to the city of Montreal, and the negotiations were resumed. It was almost decided to choose a site in the east end near Lafontaine Park; but protests were made. No arrangement having been arrived at, the Department of Militia notified the city of Montreal that it would establish the school on Lafontaine Park, which belongs to the Dominion government; but I understand that the city of Montreal object very strongly to the school being established there, and is trying to secure a site elsewhere. The city has been trying to secure some land on Montreal park, partly on the Brunet estate and partly on property that belongs to the city. That site was objected to, however, and I understand that the city is at the present moment negotiating with regard to three or four other sites which the Department of Militia will have to consider. I am not aware that any particular site has been chosen apart from the notification given by the Department of Militia to the city of Montreal that if they could not secure another site, they would have to erect the school on Lafontaine Park.
Montreal examining warehouse, $20,000.

This is mainly for elevators. There are six, and this is to complete the work.
Montreal inland revenue building-additions, repairs, &e., $50,000.
Where are you going to put that building ?

As lion, gentlemen from) Montreal who are acquainted with the present building know, it is a very old one, and understand the city has offered, if the department will extend it, to transfer to the department a small piece of ground now used as a park. I am unable to give the committee even an approximate estimate of what the building will cost. It will depend on the extent to which we can use the old building, which I understand has been built fifty or seventy-five years. In this case, I shall have to ask the committee to trust the department to incur no greater expenditure than will be necessary.
Has the government acquired the site which the city has promised -the Place Royale ?

No, simply because the department has not been able to make up its mind as to the extent of the work it can undertake. I understand that the city is prepared to transfer the site, and this Mr. PREFONTAINE.
amount is appropriated with that understanding. For the reasons I have explained, the department has not started the negotiations. They do not know what the requirements will be.
I am told that the inland revenue building is entirely too small.
That is the reason for the vote.

But the enlargement cannot be effected for the amount of the vote. I cannot understand how it is that the department has not closed the matter of the site, because it has been pending for much more than a year ? I understand that some of the neighbouring proprietors signed a petition against the site being deeded over to the government. That opposition was made, I think, over a year ago.
The first of this vote was only last session, and it was only then the department were in the position to negotiate.
Do I understand the minister to say that he has any authority for the statement that the city will provide the site ?

I do not know that I am in a position to say that I have any authority in black and white, or that I am in possession of exact information. But I know that the question of the extension of this building came up, and it was intimated to me- I do not remember by whom-that if we desired to extend the building, the city of Montreal would give a site for that purpose.

I have listened to this style of argument for a long while. In our part of the country we would not consider building until we knew where we were going to build. Yet, here we have the minister asking money for building after building, though he cannot tell us anything about the sites. We are simply voting this money blind. And, from what I know of human nature, I think the minister will find that, the announcement having been made that he intends to put up a building, he will hardly be able to secure the site except at exorbitant figures. I understand him to! state that the city of Montreal will give the site if he will agree to enlarge the building, but when he is asked for particulars, he cannot tell us anything upon which he bases that statement; he cannot tell us where he got the information, or whether he got it at all. It seems to me absurd for the minister to ask us, as representatives of the people, to vote public money when he does not know anything about where that money is to be put. The excuse is made that the building is seventy-five years old. What difference does that make ?
It is too small.

But it is no harder to enlarge a building one hundred years old

than it is to enlarge one five years old. The question is, not the age of the building, but whether it is in a good state of repair.
I have no objection to vote money for proper public buildings in this great country of ours, but X think we ought to know from the minister what the cost is to be, and not have further repetitions of what we have seen here-the minister asking for a few thousand dollars and, before the building is completed, asking for three or four times what we were led to believe the total cost would be.

I am a member of the city council of Montreal, and I think application has been made by the department for the small piece of ground that has been referred to. Speaking as a member of the city council, and judging from what I have heard other members of that body say, I think they will not hesitate to give it in order to secure this fine improvement. ' I think my bon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) will back me up in what I say.

I do not wish to suggest foi a moment that this vote is not needed. The building at present occupied by the department is a very old one, and should be exchanged for a modern building within the least possible delay. But the part I object to is the intimation on the part of the minister that the putting up of this building is conditional upon the site being provided by the city. We have voted this evening a great many appropriations for post offices and other public buildings throughout the Dominion, and in every case the site was deliberately purchased by the department. I do not think it quite fair to the city of Montreal to discriminate by saying that unless the city of Montreal provides the site this money will not be spent. The city council, I am sure, are prepared to enter into legitimate negotiations. I listened carefully to learn whether the minister had any authority on which to base his statement that the site was to be provided by the city. In regard to that statement, I have a letter from the acting city clerk of Montreal saying that he has looked up the matter of the proposed extension of the inland revenue building, and he does not find any resolution passed to furnish the land gratuitously. There are a number of matters pending to be arranged by negotiation between the city of Montreal and the government. These questions will probably be settled some day by an interview between the representatives of the city council and the various departments at Ottawa that are interested. I think it only fair to leave the city of Montreal in these negotiations free to offer the piece of land for this building. I desire to enter my protest against making this vote conditional on the city gratuitously providing a site. As the hon. member for St. Anne's (Mr. Gallery) said, I am sure the city will be ready to negotiate in a friendly spirit, but I do 36
not think you are justified in making the enlargement of the inland revenue building conditional upon the city handing over to the government a piece of valuable property.

As a member of the city council of Montreal, I remember that three or four years ago the city council made application to the government for a piece of ground, and the government were so kind as to give that ground. I do not see why the city of Montreal should now object to give the government this ground, which is of no earthly use to the city, especially when the government is going to use it to put up a good building.
I think my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) will help me in the city council, especially as the government will spend probably $100,000 in putting up this building. The present building is an eyesore. I think the city will not object to giving this property as a site for a public building.

X would ask the minister if he would have any objection to striking out) the words ' site for addition to be furnished by the city ' ? That is a discriminating proviso, and does not treat the city fairly. Strike this out, and the question of the site will be a matter of negotiation between the city and the government, and I am sure both will enter into it in a spirit of fairness. But the vote in its present form seems to say that if the city does not provide a site the building will not be constructed. That means that the consent of parliament is made conditional upon the decision of an outside and independent body.

Has my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) forgotten that the city of Montreal has received from this government already very valuable sites ? There is the Champs de Mars, there is Logan's farm and Fletcher's field handed over to the city for nothing.
I understand that the properties referred to have not been deeded over, but leased to the city.
At a nominal rental of $1 a year.

But this is a question of handing over property absolutely. I go back to the point referred to by my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane)-We are asked to vote an amount for an improvement which cannot be carried out unless the site is provided in some way or other, and, when we ask if the site is provided, the only information we have shows that no site has been secured. The building which the government has on the Place Royale is an eyesore. And the little strip of land adjoining the present building cannot be of much use to the city of Montreal. It cannot be of much use to anybody, so far as I can see, except the government. If the government secures that site and puts



up a building costing $100,000-I think it -must spend that much before that work is -ended-it seems to me the city of Montreal will get good value for what it has given.
I understood the minister to say that if the city would not give the site, no building would be put up.
I do not want to make it so strong as that.
I understood the minister at the beginning to say that.
That is what is meant by (hat condition.

I think the city of Montreal cannot afford to lose such a fine building as that. If the hon. member for St. Antoine, Montreal (Mr. Ames) will help me ihere to-night, we ought to be good for this *small piece of land.

We have to consider that this building must be in a certain place. It is at present near the custom house in the business centre, surrounded by wholesale stores and warehouses. If the city of Montreal gave a piece of land too far away, it could not be accepted, because the building has to be in the centre of the city. The present building is a small one, *on a small square. There has been a tendency in Montreal the last few years, as the members of the city council know very well, to enlarge the squares.
It cannot be done at that place.

Unless it is all taken up, and even if it were all taken up, it would still be objectionable. My impression is that the only way to solve the question would be, if the foundations of the present building are not solid enough to support two or three stories-because we are having some skyscrapers now in Montreal-if the foundations are not strong enough, it would be better to take down the old building and put up another very high one where the present one stands. That is the only way that we can have the Inland Revenue offices in the most proper place in the city, and if we went anywhere else they would not be convenient for the public. It is of no use talking about getting a piece of land from the city ; the government had better make up their minds immediately to put up a building which will be a credit to themselves and to the city.

I would like an answer from the minister whether he would object to striking out that clause in the estimate.
Mr. PREFONTAINE, It is clear from the estimate itself that the government has made up its mind to have a new building ; but if there is to be an addition to the building the city will have to furnish the *site. I know the site very well. The building is an eyesore, everybody admits that, Mr. MONK.
it must be demolished and rebuilt, and it can be rebuilt five, six or ten stories high, as need may require. But if it is thought proper to enlarge the building, and the city of Montreal is not willing to give us the extra ground, then we will have to build on the same ground. The city must understand that if they want more accommodation they must furnish the site. The place which it is in contemplation to use for an extension of the building, is perfectly useless at the present moment; it is only a place where a lot of idle people congregate, there are no trees on it. So if the city does not think proper in its own interest to give a little piece of that ground in order to have a larger building, then we shall have to renew the building as it exists. There are many precedents for cities furnishing sites for public buildings. There is an item in the estimates for a military school at Three Rivers, the site to be furnished by the city. It rests with the city council of Montreal to say whether they will take interest enough in the city to furnish the land for a larger building.

I find it necessary in discussing this question to speak not only as a member of parliament, but as an aider-man of the city of Montreal. As an aider-man, I have been cognizant that certain negotiations have been going on with the government from time to time to settle a number of matters in dispute. We are anx-* ious to secure certain favours from the government, we are anxious to secure certain privileges on St. Helen's Island, also on Lafontaine Park, also on the ancient burial ground on Papineau Avenue ; we are anxious to secure these from the government. Now it is a matter more or less of barter, in which we have some things the government wants, and we are prepared to make reasonable exchanges with the government. We have this piece of property which the government desires in order to extend one of its necessary public buildings, we are probably prepared to grant that ; but we want it to be considered as one of the commodities which we have in our barter and sale with the government. Now I want to point out that you are bringing to bear undue pressure on the city council to make them part with one of their assets, which is a valuable one when we come to the matter of settling up these difficulties with you, because you are in the position of saying that unless the city council gives you this land for nothing, the Inland Revenue Department shall continue in its present congested condition, and the citizens of Montreal shall continue to cry out, and you will say, It is not our fault, the city owns the land, and unless the city gives the land we cannot put up the building. You are therefore bringing pressure to bear upon the city council to part with one of its assets, which they are holding in view of making eventually a fair settlement with you of the various questions at issue. Further*

than that, I think you are discriminating against us, because you are voting a sum of money, the expenditure of which depends upon concurrent legislation on the part of another body over which you have no control. Unless the city council practically ratifies your decision, why, the building cannot go up. I think therefore it would be far better to strike that line from the estimates and allow that matter to be dealt with in an amicable spirit along with the other questions which are at issue between the government and the city. I am sure you will find on the part of the citizens of Montreal no desire to get the last pound of flesh, no disposition to mete out Shylock treatment to the government. But we do not wish to part with one of our assets absolutely, aside from a settlement of other outstanding questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are wasting a lot of valuable time in discussing this question. The item must pass in its present shape or not at all, because the committee has no authority to add anything to the item that is brought down, and it will add to the burdens of the country if you take that rider out, because it would add to the item the value of the site. If we pay for the site we add to the vote. You cannot do that constitutionally.
It is not a matter of payment for the site, it is a matter of exchange for the site.

The hon. gentleman forgets the most important part of the whole question. If we get the site we will extend the building; if we do not get the site rather than pay for- the site, we might possibly prefer to make the building higher. That is the gist of the whole question, and must be taken into consideration by the department.
Montreal military, buildings-new stores building, $10,000.

This is one of several military buildings that are being erected at the headquarters of the different military centres. There is one to be erected in Montreal, one in Winnipeg and one in London. They are for the purpose of storing military equipments of all kinds, and have nothing to do with armouries. At present, buildings are being rented for that purpose in certain places, and at large rents.
How many years has this item been in the estimates ?
Only last year.

I object to that principle, as I did last year. To my mind it is a very bad principle for the government to follow. The government either require that money for expenditure or they do not; if they do not require it they should not have it. If it is not intended to expend it, but to keep it on the estimates dangling before the 36i	<
people, it is always available when elections come on, though it may never be used-I say that is an unsound principle. The government should not ask for anything they do not intend to spend.
Has anything been done to that building yet ?
No. I think there are somej negotiations going on with the permanent corps in Montreal. I have no objection to let the matter stand.
I do not know anything about it.

This item is for erecting a stone building in the city of Montreal for the purpose of receiving the militia stores. Ten thousand dollars was put in the estimates last year but we have been unable to obtain a site. We have not started negotiations for a site for the building. If the committee desire me I am satisfied to let it stand.

I am not objecting to the expenditure of the money. If the government desire to spend the money and are prepared to spend it, all right. I am not objecting to the item at all but I am objecting to the principle of voting money year after year for three or four years as we have been doing in this case and not a dollar of the money spent.
We are so economical. Why should you be pressing us to spend money ?

I am not pressing you to spend money but I am objecting to the improper course of asking for money that you do not intend to spend. The government ought first to make up their minds that they intend to spend so much money on a public building, ask parliament for it and, if it is granted, expend it. But, if there is no definite object in view to have an item in the estimates dangling before the public it is wrong.
There is no doubt that would be wrong, but this item was put in the estimates only last year and it is being revoted now.
I asked if it were put in before last year and the answer was ' yes.'
No, the answer was not ' yes.'
I understood the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Pre-fontaine) to say ' yes.'
I said that it was put in last year.
It was passed last year.

I can understand that you might pass over a single year without

te *expending the money, but we have many items that are voted two or three years when no expenditures are made.
This is in connection with the Montreal barracks, and no site has been chosen because this building is to be put near the barracks for the permanent force.
When the matter of the barracks is decided this will follow ?
Yes.

Not necessarily. I would not like to say that.
Montreal post office-improvements, $25,000.

This is for the purpose of improving the front of the Montreal post office and giving more accommodation. This vote is asked for by the Post Office Department for the extension of the front of the building to make more accommodation downstairs.	-
There is very serious ground of complaint as to the size of the post office.
This is foi the purpose of extending it.
How can you extend it unless you add another story V
There is a certain area between the front walk and the door which it is intended to take into the building, so that it may be used for post office purposes.
What is the plan of the building ?
The plan is not yet completed although nearly so.
And that will cost $5,000 ?
It will cost $25,000.
I do not understand without having seen the plan how you can make an enlargement of the building there?

There is an open vestibule in front of the building. It is intended to move the main wall out in front and include the open space which now forms the vestibule in the building so as to increase the accommodation.
Mr. BERGEkON. It will be down on the steps then.
No, there is a lot of space in front. There will be just double the floor space.
Can the hon. minister give us the additional floor space that will be created ?
The lobby at present is 85 x 15. It will give about 85 x 15 feet extra space.

This will be the proper time to find out whether there is going to be a new post office in the city of Montreal. Instead of spending $25,000 to do something which I think will not improve the appearance of the present building and which will not give much additional accommodation would it not be better to adopt the view which has prevailed in Montreal for a long time that a new post office should be erected in the eastern part of Montreal ? My hon. friend the Postmaster General will perhaps remember that the other night we had a very long talk about that. His answers to me showed that he was not very well posted because I had the honour to receive a note from him afterwards explaining that some of the answers were not quite correct. I want to remind you, Mr. Chairman, that there is nothing in these estimates for a new post office. The item for the new postal station has nothing to do with the question I am putting to the government as to whether a new post office building will be erected in the eastern part of Montreal. I stated the other night that there has long been talk of such a building in St. James division of Montreal. It has been very truly said that the present post office is entirely inadequate to the demands of the service in Montreal and we were led to understand in some little political meetings we had in St. James division during the last two or three years that such a building would be erected. I believe there was some correspondence between the government and the representative of St. James division (Mr. Gervais) to that effect, although, of course, he can speak more authoritatively on that subject than I can. This is the proper time to find out whether the government intend to have such a building erected in the eastern part of Montreal, either in St. James, or in St. Mary's division, or anywhere in the eastern part of Montreal.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend (Mr. Bergeron) takes exception to the accommodation furnished by the present building on St. James Street, Montreal. It is quite true that the building to-day is not adequate to the demands upon it owing to the growth and prosperity of the city and to the increased volume of mail matter, but the congestion at the central office will be relieved and entirely done away with when we carry out the policy we have in view of erecting a postal station near the Bonaventure station and enlarging the vestibule of the present building on St. James street. My hon. friend, if he has a plan of that building in his mind, will remember that when you seek to enter the building you first of all ascend a flight of stairs and then there is a space

*between the street line and the entrance of the building of perhaps 12 or 15 feet.
Ten feet, I think.

I cannot say how many, but it is quite a substantial space. It is proposed, I think, to include that space in the lobby ; that is the part of the post office which is available for the general public to enter there to transact postal business. When that improvement is made it will afford very great advantage and accommodation to the people. Then, when the Bonaventure postal station is established there will be a large amount of mail that comes in and leaves Montreal that will never pass through the main post office on St. James street at all. That will get the go-by. For example, newspapers and parcels will practically all be handled at the postal station opposite Bonaventure station. Moreover, a large quantity of the ordinary mail matter which comes in to be distributed throughout the city of Montreal, instead of being sent up to the main office to be there rehandled and sorted and given to the mail carriers, will be dealt with at the postal station, and from that point the letter-carriers will serve a considerable part of the district immediately around Bonaventure station. This will very greatly relieve the condition of affairs at the main post office.
Will that be a building ?
It will, of course, be a building in which whatever post office work is transacted at any post office will be transacted.
What will be the size?
I could not say. I do not know if the lot has been secured, there has been some trouble. The minister says that the lot has been secured on Cathedral Street opposite the Grand Trunk station.
I may state that the lot has been secured, because I know that the owner has been paid for it.

I would ask the Postmaster General to explain the situation here. When this new postal station is established- which will, I understand, relieve to a large extent the central post office-and the contemplated improvements are made at an expenditure of $25,000, does the Postmaster General think that that will relieve the con gestion for a number of years? I do not re-1 gard the expenditure of $25,000 as being very large in this connection at all, but still it would be a pity to expend that $25,000 to make improvements which might prove insufficient within a few years.

If it was only patchwork that was proposed such a proposition would be open to question, but today in the advanced and progressive postoffice world-and we claim to be a part of that world-the old system of having a
grand pile for post office work is being abandoned; instead of having all the work
of distributing the mail matter concentrated at one point, the policy now is to have substations at different points and aS a city grows to multiply your substations and to despatch the mail matter from the incoming trains to those substations for distribution to the district immediately around, and, of course, in like manner to collect out-going mail matter from different points and deliver it from the substations to the railways without its ever passing through the main post office. I have no doubt in the world that the day of large post offices, great architectural piles, is a thing of the past so far as Canada is concerned. This will be a good and wise expenditure, and if in time the progress of the city demands more postal accommodation, it would not be to the interest of the mail service to supply that accommodation by erecting a larger building in one spot, rather by erecting substations throughout the city.

I have had the advantage of hearing the Postmaster General before dealing with this question of decentralization. I quite approve of it and I thought that when the Postmaster General began he was going to answer the question I asked, but, unfortunately, like many hon. gentlemen he has mystified himself in a multitude of words and has not answered the question which I asked ; he has not done what I think he intended to do when he got up. I asked the Postmaster General to tell the committee whether, when that expenditure of $25,000 is made upon the central post office in Montreal, having regard to the tact that there is a policy of decentralization, and that another substation is to be established to relieve the congestion, we would have all that Montreal would require at that particular point for several years to come or whether this small addition to the Montreal central post office would be found adequate only for a short season of time. I was not talking about ' great monumental piles ' or anything elaborate. I was speaking about what I understand the city of Montreal as a great commercial centre would require. I want to know from the Postmaster General, and I think we should know that distinctly, is this to be a wise expenditure in this sense that it will meet the requirements of Montreal at that point for some years to come ?
I think it will.

I do not share the opinion of the Postmaster General on this point. I really- believe it would be a great deal better not to vote $25,000 for that purpose. In view of what the Postmaster General said before about the policy of decentralizing post offices, I would think it would

be better to spend a little more in different parts of the city. We are going to build a station near the Bonaventure railway station, I understand from the Postmaster General, and I think that is a very good idea ; I believe it will be money well spent. We have many railway stations in Montreal. Montreal is a terminal. We have not one railway that goes through Montreal, properly speaking. If we are to have one station at Bonaventure which will serve both Windsor station, the terminus of the C.P.R. and Bonaventure station, the terminus of the G.T.R. and the I.O.R., why not have one post office station at the Place Viger station in the eastern portion of the city of Montreal. When I speak of the eastern portion I am not, speaking of that part of Montreal in a particular way. I join with my hon. friend in his idea of enlarging the facilities for the distributing of mail in Montreal, but we are here going to spend $25,000 that in my mind will not be well spent. I am afraid we are going to disfigure the present post! office, which is a handsome building, and it will not attain the results the minister hopes to obtain.
Sir WILLIAM MULOCIv. What do you mean?

Because it will not give you increased room commensurate with the amount of money you will spend on it, and if you would only spend a little more and put a substation near the Place Viger station you would have three distributing centres, the central office and the two railway stations at the two ends of Montreal. I believe that was the idea the hon. member for East Simcoe had in his mind when he put that famous question to the Postmaster General.

If it were the case that this expenditure would not add to the accommodation furnished the public I would agree with what my hon. friend says, but the architect informs me at this moment that this expenditure will give a floor space available to the public of 2,000 feet, as against the present floor space of 1,200 feet. The present space available for the public is 80 feet by 15 feet, and my hon. friend can multiply and determine that amount himself.
It is no use multiplying ; I do not believe the figures are correct.

I give the figures of the architect, who must know what he is talking about. The present space is 1,200 square feet and this will give 2,000 square feet.

Before this item is passed, I would like to make a few remarks.
I would like to acquaint the House with Mr. BERGERON.
this fact, that the condition of affairs in Montreal, as far as postal facilities in the constituency of St. James are concerned, has become unbearable. I represent the constituency of St. James, and in this electoral division you will find 43,000 inhabitants. Adjoining that constituency you find the electoral district of St. Mary and that of St. Louis, and if you add together the inhabitants of these three wards, you will find that they contain over 117,000 inhabitants. I think this is unfair treatment to the east of Montreal, and it cannot be suffered to continue. I know quite well that the Postmaster General of Canada, under section 36 of chapter 35 of the Revised Statutes, has to decide whether or not it would be useful to establish a sub post office in Montreal east; I know quite well also that it is the duty of the Minister of Public Works to build such a post office; and this is the reason I am bringing this question forward tonight; because I want to know, in the first place, from the hon. Postmaster General whether he has made up his mind that this is the proper time to give adequate postal facilities to the east of Montreal, and whether it is the intention of the Minister of Public Works to build a sub-post office there. You must bear in mind that the east of Montreal has built up a trade larger than that of Montreal west. On this point I refer the hon. Postmaster General to the letter which has been sent to him by Mr. Jones, the cashier of the Quebec Bank; I refer him also to the resolution which was unanimously adopted by the Montreal city council, recommending the erection of a subpost office in the east of Montreal. You will find either in or close to that constituency one branch of the Bank of Montreal, two branches of the Bank of Hochelaga, one branch of the Montreal City and District Savings Bank, one branch of the Quebec Bank, one branch of the Moisons Bank, and two branches of the Provincial Bank of Canada. I may remind the hon. Postmaster General that most of the newspapers in Montreal have recommended the expenditure. Do you know that the business men of the east of Montreal have to take the street car or drive or walk one mile and a half to buy five or six stamps? We want in Montreal east the postal facilities which every good post office to-day affords to the people. We want a good sub-post office in which

money orders will be issued at which our letters will be received, from which our letters will be distributed, in which a savings bank business will be done, in which a letter may be insured, in which we shall be able to secure a service of late mailable matter, and from which we could enjoy a special delivery service. We want for the electors of St. James division, as well as those of St. Mary's and part of the St. Lawrence division, these postal facilities. We do not wish to suffer any longer the conditions of affairs which I have described. We want the government to spend in the east of Montreal at least as much as it is spending in Montreal west. St. Anne's.

area of 9,769 square feet. The second lot is 98 feet by 33 feet.

In the post office building in Montreal. The usual methods were I adopted-advertisement inserted in the

I notice we are building hospitals for the treatment of trachoma, one down in the maritime provinces this year, and we are also proposing a building in Montreal for the treatment of the same disease. Of course I am aware that a matter like this can only be exhaustibly treated! when the estimates of the Department of the Interior are under consideration. But I wish to protest strongly against this expenditure. It is altogether the result of the careless policy we have adopted in regard to immigration. The spread of trachoma throughout Canada is so great as to constitute a national danger. If my hon. friend will inquire in Montreal from the specialists for eye diseases at the Royal Victoria hospital, he will find that that disease is now implanted in Canada. I have here the annual report of the Commissioner General of Immigration for the United States, for last year, and it points out, with! details, liow diseased persons are now entering the United States, and describes the measures that have been taken to prevent them from entering from Canada. During the year 1903, they refused, in all American ports, 1,700 immigrants affected with contagious diseases, of whom 1,400 came from! Canada, and were therefore sent back intol Canada.
